title: Did Xuanzang, Tang China's Most Famous Monk, Leave the Country Illegally?
description:
In 629, Li Chang, a clerk in Guazhou, laid a warrant from Liangzhou before a young monk: "There is a monk named Xuanzang who intends to go to the western lands. All prefectures and counties shall keep strict watch and seize him." This episode follows the order of the Ci'en Biography: the petition in Chang'an, where the biography says "an edict refused it," while Daoxuan's Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks, written by a contemporary, says it was never forwarded at all; Liangzhou's governor Li Daliang ordering him back to Chang'an, after which he "hid by day and traveled by night"; Li Chang tearing up the warrant in front of him; the guide Shi Pantuo taking him around the gate ten li upstream of the Yumen Pass; a beacon tower's arrow that "nearly hit his knee," the spilled water bag, and "better to die going west than live going back east"; and King Qu Wentai of Gaochang swearing brotherhood with him (Journey to the West gives that role to Emperor Taizong). On the way home, in a memorial sent from Khotan, he wrote it himself: "I defied the statutes and went privately to India." In the second month of 645 he met Taizong at Luoyang Palace. Taizong asked, "Master, why did you not tell me when you left?" He answered that he had gone on his own, "the crime of acting without authority." Taizong said, "There is no need for shame." Leaving without the court's permission: he admitted it himself. Filed. Which year he set out: most Tang records say 629; only one memorial, preserved in the Guang Hongming Ji, says 627. Unresolved.

Buddhist texts follow CBETA (Taishō base text, with collation notes); the dynastic histories, the Zizhi Tongjian, the Tang Code with commentary and Journey to the West follow the Daizhige transcriptions. In the Taishō base text, the character for "edict" in "an edict refused it" appears in a variant form. The Tang Code is a later statute; the law in force when Xuanzang crossed the border has not survived. Sources are listed in the references below. The episode covers the journey and where the texts come from, and does not comment on faith.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

xz101.text: Leaving in 629, he reached Guazhou, on Tang China's western edge.

xz102.text: A clerk named Li Chang quietly took a document to a young monk.

xz103.text: It said: a monk named Xuanzang wants to go west; every district must watch and arrest him.

xz104.text: Li Chang asked just one thing: Master, isn't this you?

xz107.text: Below a beacon tower past the Yumen Pass, an arrow flew at him.

xz108.text: In Journey to the West, his sworn brother is Taizong. In the records, who was it?

xz109.text: Years later, writing to the emperor, he put down eight characters himself.

xz110.text: Back home, what was the first thing the emperor asked him?

xz111.text: Did Tang China's most famous monk really leave illegally?

xz201.text: At first he did ask the court: in Chang'an, he and a few companions petitioned to go west.

xz202.text: His disciples' Ci'en Biography says: an edict refused them.

xz203.text: The others gave up; only he refused to quit.

xz204.text: But did that petition ever reach the emperor?

xz205.text: Daoxuan, who met him, is gentler in Continued Biographies:

xz206.text: He filed alone; no office forwarded it;

xz207.text: so in this version, no edict said no.

xz208.text: Either way, he set off anyway.

xz209.text: In Liangzhou he taught for over a month. Then trouble:

xz210.text: The Ci'en Biography says the young Tang barred commoners from leaving.

xz211.text: Governor Li Daliang, newly ordered, watched closely.

xz212.text: Word came: a monk from Chang'an meant to go west.

xz213.text: Alarmed, Li summoned him. He said: to seek the Dharma.

xz214.text: Li ordered him back to Chang'an.

xz216.text: No. A Liangzhou master secretly sent two disciples to sneak him west.

xz217.text: From then on, afraid to travel openly, he hid by day and moved by night to Guazhou.

xz218.text: In Guazhou he learned: the road west had to pass the Yumen Pass.

xz219.text: Beyond it were five beacons, 100 li apart, with no water or grass between.

xz220.text: Then the warrant from the opening arrived from Liangzhou.

xz221.text: Asked by Li Chang, he didn't deny it; he told the truth.

xz222.text: Li said: if you truly can do it, I'll destroy this for you.

xz223.text: He tore it up before the monk's eyes and urged: Master, leave soon.

xz224.text: The Yumen Pass still stood ahead.

xz225.text: Tang rules required a pass permit called a guosuo.

xz226.text: How does a wanted man get through?

xz301.text: He avoided the gate. His guide was Shi Pantuo, a Central Asian who came to the temple to pray.

xz302.text: He promised to guide the monk past the five beacons.

xz303.text: He also brought an old Central Asian man, who warned: the western road is deadly; no one gets through.

xz304.text: Unable to sway him, the old man traded him an old red horse: 15 round trips to Yiwu, it knew the way. Remember it.

xz305.text: At the third watch they crept to the river, the Yumen Pass in sight.

xz306.text: Ten li upstream, Shi bridged it with logs, grass and sand, and drove the horses across.

xz307.text: Later Tang law: no papers at the gate, a year's penal labor; bypassing the gate, one grade more.

xz308.text: The law of his own day hasn't survived.

xz309.text: So did anyone ever punish him for this?

xz310.text: Soon Shi rose with a knife toward the monk, then turned back within ten steps.

xz311.text: The biography says the monk couldn't tell why, and suspected treachery.

xz312.text: At dawn, knife out and bow drawn, Shi told the monk to go first. He refused.

xz313.text: After a while Shi said: I'm not going on; my family is big, and I can't break the law.

xz314.text: The monk swore: even if cut to dust, he'd never betray him. They parted there.

xz315.text: From here, alone with the old horse, he walked into the desert.

xz316.text: Alone, could he make it out?

xz317.text: At the first beacon he crept to water and drank.

xz318.text: He got out his waterskin; from the dark, something flew.

xz401.text: It was the arrow from the start; in the dark, it nearly hit his knee.

xz402.text: A second came. He shouted: I'm a monk from the capital, don't shoot!

xz403.text: Officer Wang Xiang urged: I'm from Dunhuang, let's go there.

xz404.text: Wang added: you won't be punished today.

xz406.text: He replied: detain me or sentence me, but I won't take one step east.

xz407.text: Wang gave him water and food, wept goodbye, pointed him to the fourth.

xz408.text: Wang's kin at the fourth said: skip the fifth, they're rough;

xz409.text: go 100 li to Wild Horse Spring.

xz410.text: So of those five beacons, he actually entered only two.

xz411.text: Next came the Moheyan Desert: over 800 li, no birds above, no beasts below, no water or grass.

xz412.text: But after 100-odd li, he got lost and couldn't find Wild Horse Spring.

xz413.text: Dismounting to drink, he lost grip of the heavy bag, and it all spilled.

xz414.text: As the biography puts it: his supply for 1,000 li, gone at once.

xz415.text: He turned east, back toward the fourth.

xz418.text: He told himself: better to die going west than to live going back east.

xz419.text: He turned his horse and went northwest again.

xz420.text: Four nights and five days without a drop of water; he collapsed on the sand, unable to go on.

xz421.text: On the fifth midnight, a cool wind rose, like a plunge into cold water.

xz423.text: The biography says it led him to green grass beside a clear pool.

xz424.text: Could he make it out alone? He did. Two days later he left the desert and reached Yiwu.

xz425.text: Gaochang's king Qu Wentai sent for him.

xz426.text: The king wanted him as royal teacher. He refused, fasting 3 days, not even water.

xz428.text: On day four, the king gave in.

xz429.text: Before the Buddha and queen mother, they became brothers.

xz430.text: Answer to the opening question: his real sworn brother was Gaochang's king.

xz431.text: In the novel, what did the Guazhou warrant become?

xz432.text: A travel pass Taizong gave him when seeing him off.

xz433.text: The king gave funds for 20 years, 24 letters of introduction,

xz434.text: and wrote to the Western Turk Yabghu Khagan: the Master is my brother.

xz435.text: He promised: on the way back, 3 years in Gaochang.

xz501.text: No. Leaving India, he told a king he'd go north to keep his date in Gaochang;

xz502.text: But back in 640, Tang had already destroyed Gaochang.

xz503.text: At Khotan he wrote Taizong; the Ci'en Biography has it.

xz504.text: Those eight characters are in it:

xz505.text: "I defied the statutes and went privately to India": he broke the law and left on his own.

xz506.text: In the same memorial he also wrote, as was customary: the emperor's might cleared every road.

xz507.text: Sent to Chang'an, how would the emperor reply?

xz508.text: Seven or eight months on, word came: Taizong said come at once.

xz509.text: Hurrying, he reached Chang'an in the 1st month of 645.

xz510.text: Tang texts all say he was away across seventeen years.

xz511.text: But the emperor was in Luoyang, readying war in Liaodong.

xz512.text: In month 2, at Luoyang's Yiluan Hall, he met Taizong.

xz513.text: Taizong's first words, as promised, were:

xz514.text: Master, why leave without a word to me?

xz515.text: He said: I petitioned two or three times, was refused, so I went alone.

xz516.text: Going off unauthorized was a crime, he said; he was deeply ashamed.

xz517.text: Taizong said: a monk risking his life for the Dharma to benefit all, I admire. No need for shame.

xz518.text: Punished? Per the Ci'en Biography, that one line pardoned him to his face.

xz519.text: So which year did he leave?

xz520.text: Most records give 629, as at the start;

xz521.text: only one memorial attributed to him says 627.

xz522.text: So, in this file: leaving illegally, on record; the year he left, unresolved.

xz523.text: As Li Chang, would you have torn up that warrant?

xz524.text: We only tell what the records show. Subscribe to open files with us.
